title: Rommel's dash to the wire
pull: He left the battle to win it

facts.text: On 23 November 1941, Totensonntag, the Afrika Korps overran the 5th South African Brigade at Sidi Rezegh. It was a victory, but it cost the Germans 72 of their 162 tanks, losses they could not replace.

The Afrika Korps commander, Lt. Gen. Ludwig Crüwell, wanted to stay and finish off the British armor on the battlefield. Rommel judged that the British were off balance and that the moment for a bold stroke had come.

His idea was to drive deep behind the British to the Egyptian frontier wire, relieve the Axis garrisons there, and break the Eighth Army's nerve. He remembered how sensitive the British had been to roaming armor at Mechili in April and in Operation Battleaxe in June.
Waving aside Crüwell's objections, Rommel set off at 10 a.m. on 24 November at the head of the 21st Panzer Division, with the 15th Panzer following at noon.

The columns covered about 60 miles in six hours and reached the frontier near Gasr el Abid at about 4 p.m. In the British rear, supply trucks and headquarters fled east in panic, and the aircraft of the Eighth Army commander, Lt. Gen. Alan Cunningham, was shelled as it took off.

The gamble rested on the British losing their nerve. Cunningham had already been ready to call off the offensive, but General Sir Claude Auchinleck, at Eighth Army headquarters, ordered the attack on Tobruk to go on.
Leading from the front, Rommel was out of touch with his own army. That night he and Crüwell lost their way and spent it almost alone on the British side of the wire, narrowly escaping capture.
The columns drove past large British supply dumps near Gabr Saleh. Capturing them might have kept the raid going, but the Germans never found them.
While the panzers roamed the frontier, the New Zealand Division pushed toward Tobruk. By the evening of 25 November the 15th Panzer Division was down to 53 tanks.

On 27 November the Afrika Korps had to head back toward Tobruk. The dash had failed. Auchinleck replaced Cunningham with Maj. Gen. Neil Ritchie, and on 7 to 8 December Rommel lifted the siege of Tobruk.

declassified.fact: One raiding column drove straight into the British No. 50 Field Maintenance Centre south of Sidi Omar early on 25 November and scattered most of its staff. By afternoon the Germans were gone, little damage had been done, they had found hardly any of the well hidden petrol, and the day's supply convoys were unloading as usual.

body:
Rommel's plan was to drive straight past the British into their rear and break their nerve. By nightfall he was lost on the wrong side of the wire.

24 November 1941. A day after a costly win at Sidi Rezegh, Rommel overruled the Afrika Korps commander, Ludwig Crüwell, who wanted to stay and finish the British armor. At 10 a.m. he set off at the head of the 21st Panzer Division for the Egyptian frontier. The columns covered about 60 miles in six hours. British supply trucks and headquarters fled east, and the Eighth Army commander's aircraft was shelled as it took off.

But General Auchinleck ordered the attack on Tobruk to go on. Within days the panzers had to turn back, and on 7 to 8 December Rommel lifted the siege of Tobruk.
